analysis.one_liner: Requires automakers to sell a rising share of zero-emission cars, reaching 100% by 2040.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in November 2018 with two cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Clean Air Act to require every vehicle manufacturer to make a rising share of its U.S. new-car sales zero-emission vehicles: 50% by 2030, climbing each year to 100% by 2040, after which only zero-emission cars could be sold. Manufacturers could meet the targets by selling clean cars or by buying credits from companies that sell more than their share, and would face civil penalties for missing the targets. The bill would leave state zero-emission rules in place and be enforced by the EPA.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people gain cleaner air and a faster shift away from gasoline cars, plus the lower fuel and maintenance costs of electric vehicles. Communities near highways and ports, which bear the worst vehicle pollution, gain the most. Manufacturers that have already invested in electric vehicles gain a guaranteed market and a new revenue stream in the form of credits they can sell to slower-moving competitors.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers, roadside communities, and electric-car makers

how_it_helps.text: Sets a hard schedule — 50% zero-emission sales by 2030, 100% by 2040 — so the shift to clean cars cannot stall with each administration.
Backs the mandate with real teeth: civil penalties equal to twice the value of missing credits, and after 2040 the EPA can injunction-stop any manufacturer still building combustion cars.
Preserves states' authority to set their own stricter vehicle-emission and zero-emission rules, so California-style programs remain in force.
Allows partial credits for plug-in hybrids and very fuel-efficient cars, giving manufacturers a compliance ramp rather than an overnight switch.

analysis.who_pays: Vehicle manufacturers bear the compliance cost — retooling plants, developing electric models, or buying credits — and much of that cost would likely be passed into the price of new gasoline cars during the transition. The oil industry loses a shrinking share of the transportation-fuel market as the electric share grows. Consumers who rely on used cars are not directly affected, since the rule applies only to new-vehicle sales.
analysis.who_pays_short: Automakers, and gasoline-car buyers during the transition

drawbacks.text: Mandates on manufacturers tend to show up in sticker prices, so new gasoline and hybrid cars would likely cost more during the decade-long transition, which falls hardest on buyers who can only afford new entry-level vehicles.

The bill relies on a tradable credit market: a manufacturer can comply by buying credits instead of selling clean cars, which lets wealthier or further-along competitors profit while slower companies delay their own transition — a design some critics call a loophole, though the same design is what made California's program workable.

The bill sets vehicle requirements but funds nothing: no charging-station buildout, no help for lower-income buyers, and no grid upgrades — the transition's success would depend entirely on the private market and other laws.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health and climate benefits of a firm, dated phaseout of new gasoline cars are large, and the phaseout applies only to new-vehicle sales, leaving today's used-car market untouched. The honest costs are higher new-car prices during the transition and a credit market that lets some manufacturers pay instead of build. A fair assessment: strong public benefit, real transition costs, and a design that would have needed funding and infrastructure bills alongside it to work smoothly.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the Zero-Emission Vehicles Act of 2018 on November 28, 2018, near the end of the 115th Congress.

The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works; no hearing, markup, or vote followed, and no further action appears in the record before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

The bill never advanced beyond its introduction stage, so the 50%-by-2030 and 100%-by-2040 sales requirements, the credit market, and the penalty provisions were never debated or voted on in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers and the oil industry came out ahead: no manufacturer faces the 50%-by-2030 sales requirement, the credit-purchase obligation, or civil penalties, and gasoline remains the dominant new-car fuel with no federal phaseout schedule.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was entirely Democratic and Independent (one Democrat sponsor, one Democrat and one Independent cosponsor), and the Republican-run committee never took the bill up; there is no roll call to break down.

industries.note: Established manufacturers would face binding sales quotas, retooling costs, and penalties — but the same mandate creates a guaranteed market for any company that builds electric cars, and a credit-trading market that lets leaders (such as Tesla) sell credits to laggards. Automakers' resistance to the bill ran against the public's interest in cleaner air and cheaper-to-run cars.

A 100% zero-emission requirement for new cars by 2040 steadily removes the industry's largest market — transportation fuel. The industry's interest in stopping the bill ran against the public's interest in cleaner air.
The quota guarantees growing demand for their products and creates a salable credit for every clean vehicle sold. Their gain comes alongside the public's gain in vehicle emissions reductions.
